evals.prompt: Use go-security to define security policy for a multi-tenant report export. Human users authenticate through a browser session; service clients use bearer tokens. The gateway currently copies X-Tenant-ID into the request, handlers accept /tenants/{tenant}/reports/{report}, and the proposal treats any user with role=admin as allowed. Exports accept JSON filters and a customer callback URL, enqueue durable work containing the original bearer token, read report rows through a cache keyed only by report ID, call a paid rendering provider, and send the callback after following redirects. Operators want request bodies, callback URLs, provider errors, and tokens in debug logs. No CORS/CSRF/session, object/property authorization, callback authenticity, secret rotation, egress/private-IP, abuse/cost, audit, dependency, or negative-path policy exists. Write a compact threat-control specification with explicit enforcement and proof; do not redesign service topology or handler wiring.
evals.expected_output: A fail-closed security specification that separately defines authentication, authorization, tenant binding, object ownership, browser controls, input and egress defenses, scoped secrets, sensitive-data isolation, abuse budgets, auditability, dependency assumptions, and negative no-side-effect proof.
assertions: Maps browser, gateway, service-token, queue, cache, rendering-provider, and callback trust boundaries with attacker paths, assets, enforcement owners, and fail behavior
Separates authentication of caller and subject from action authorization, trusted tenant membership, report object ownership, property scope, and delegated admin scope
Rejects X-Tenant-ID, role=admin alone, and path identity as sufficient tenant or object authorization evidence and requires fail-closed authoritative checks
Defines browser session lifecycle, secure cookie behavior, origin-specific credentialed CORS, CSRF protection for ambient authority, and safe redirect or error semantics
Requires bounded strict input handling and SSRF controls across scheme, destination, DNS, redirects, connected IP, private or control-plane ranges, and authenticated callbacks

Rejects durable raw bearer-token propagation and debug secret or body logging; requires scoped credentials, approved secret source, rotation or revocation, tenant-scoped cache keys, minimization, encryption where required, retention, and redaction

Defines principal, tenant, operation, concurrency, body, attempt, and provider-cost gates before expensive work or side effects while leaving legitimate service-capacity policy to reliability or performance

Requires auditable allow, deny, and admin actions plus negative tests for unauthenticated, unauthorized, cross-tenant, non-owner, malformed or injected, replay, secret-leak, egress, and exhaustion paths with no forbidden enqueue, cache read, provider call, or callback
Records third-party and dependency or supply-chain assumptions and treats scanners as complementary to behavioral security proof

A follow-up only renames a private Go helper and changes none of those facts.
evals.expected_output: No new security decision, with every accepted trust, access, data, abuse, egress, audit, dependency, and proof constraint unchanged.
assertions: Returns no_new_decision_required or an explicit statement that accepted security constraints remain unchanged
Does not redesign authentication, authorization, tenant or object ownership, browser controls, secrets, egress, abuse, audit, dependencies, or proof
Leaves the private helper rename to implementation ownership without padding or generic security warnings

evals.prompt: Apply go-security and route only the remaining decision. Authentication, action authorization, trusted tenant binding, object and property ownership, admin scope, browser controls, input validation, SSRF and callback policy, secret handling, sensitive-data isolation, audit events, negative tests, and principal or tenant abuse and provider-cost gates are accepted and unchanged. The unresolved question is how the service should admit legitimate peak traffic, bound its general work queue, preserve its end-to-end deadline, degrade optional rendering, drain on shutdown, and roll back when capacity guardrails fail.
evals.expected_output: Only the forced security constraints remain; go-reliability owns legitimate-capacity admission, deadline, degradation, drain, and rollback policy, with no duplicate security design.
assertions: Names go-reliability as the owner of the remaining legitimate-capacity, deadline, degradation, lifecycle, and rollback decisions
Carries only the accepted principal or tenant abuse, provider-cost, fail-closed, and no-forbidden-side-effect constraints
Does not reopen or conflate authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, object ownership, or abuse policy with general reliability admission
